subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Write the reaction of i) aromatic and ii) aliphatic 1° amines with nitrous acid.

verification.note: Unit 18 (Organic Compounds Containing Nitrogen) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.115-120, from the shaded sub-box "ORGANIC COMPOUNDS CONTAINING NITROGEN" of printed chapter 12 ("12. ORGANIC CHEMISTRY"); the book prints this question on book p.117 as SAQ 6. The 2+2 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. EQUATION CHECKED: C₆H₅NH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + NaCl + 2H₂O balances C 6/6, H 9/9, N 2/2, Na 1/1, Cl 2/2, O 2/2; the book prints this equation and it is correct. The overall aliphatic reaction CH₃NH₂ + HNO₂ → CH₃OH + N₂ + H₂O balances C 1/1, H 6/6, N 2/2, O 2/2. BOOK WORDING: the printed answer calls the aliphatic product an "aliphatic di-azonium salt"; it is an alkanediazonium salt, and "di-azonium" reads as though two diazonium groups were present. The card writes alkanediazonium. BOOK GAP, filled here: the printed answer gives 273-283 K for the aromatic case but never says WHY the aromatic salt survives that temperature while the aliphatic one does not — the –N₂⁺ group on a benzene ring is stabilised by delocalisation into the ring, and there is no such stabilisation on an alkyl chain.

steps.label: Aromatic 1° amine
lines: Nitrous acid is made in the flask from NaNO₂
and HCl, because HNO₂ itself is unstable.
Aniline is treated with it at 273-283 K.
The salt is stable at 273-283 K because the
–N₂⁺ group is delocalised into the ring.
Above 283 K it decomposes to phenol.
steps.why: Nitrous acid supplies the nitrosonium ion, which converts the –NH₂ group into –N₂⁺. Keeping the flask in ice at 273-283 K is not a detail: the diazonium salt is stable only in that narrow band, and warming it puts phenol in the flask instead.
common_mistakes: Writing HNO₃ instead of HNO₂. Nitric acid is a different reagent; nitrous acid is made from NaNO₂ and HCl.
Leaving out the temperature. 273-283 K is part of the marked answer for the aromatic case.
steps.memory_tip: Ice-cold sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid on aniline gives the diazonium salt at 273-283 K.
steps.margin_note: Write 273-283 K over the arrow and the words benzenediazonium chloride under the product.

steps.label: Aliphatic 1° amine
lines: The same reagent converts an aliphatic
This salt is unstable even at 273 K and
Nitrogen gas is given off steadily, which
is used as a test for an aliphatic 1° amine.
steps.why: An alkyl group offers no way of spreading the positive charge of the –N₂⁺ group, so the alkanediazonium ion loses nitrogen as soon as it forms. The aromatic salt survives because the ring spreads that charge by delocalisation. Both amines make the same kind of salt; only its lifetime differs.
common_mistakes: Writing a stable aliphatic diazonium salt as the final product. It decomposes at once; the products are the alcohol and nitrogen gas.
Giving the same conditions and the same outcome for both cases. The difference in stability is the point of the question.
steps.memory_tip: The ring stabilises the diazonium group in the cold; a plain alkyl chain does not, so nitrogen gas comes off straight away.
steps.margin_note: Write both stages, then the overall equation. Naming the steady nitrogen gas as a test is worth one line.

insider_note: Both amines make a diazonium salt; the answer is about how long each one lasts. The aromatic salt survives at 273-283 K because the ring spreads the charge, while the aliphatic one decomposes at once to the alcohol and nitrogen gas. Losing the temperature range loses a mark on its own.
